title: When a neighbor's cup breaks
hook: when someone else's cup breaks we say "these things happen," so say it of your own (Enchiridion 26)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was obol, the small coin that buys the lettuce. Your line was I kept the coin.

A friend texts: I dented my car backing out of the garage. Your reply takes four seconds. Oh no! Happens to everyone. Is anyone hurt? That's what matters. Wise, calm, kind. A week later you dent your own car backing out of your own garage, and for the next hour you're a different person. Idiot. How could I. This always happens to me. Same kind of dent, same kind of morning. Section twenty-six of the handbook says the wisdom you need was in that four-second text.
screen: `A FRIEND'S DENTED CAR.` → `HAPPENS TO EVERYONE.` → `THEN IT'S YOUR CAR.`

segments.voice: What nature intends, Epictetus says, we can learn from the cases where we all agree. Not from arguments, but from our own easy answers about other people's troubles. When someone else's servant breaks a cup, people are quick to say: these things happen. So, he says, when your own cup breaks, be the same as you were when the other one broke. That's all. Borrow your own good advice. Then he carries it further, gently but firmly. When someone else's child or spouse dies, everyone says: that's the human lot. But when it's one's own, right away it's: oh, poor me, how wretched. We ought to remember, he says, how we felt when we heard the same news about others. Here it's worth slowing down, because this is a hard line to hear. Epictetus asks a great deal: the same steadiness for your own loss as for a stranger's. Not every reader will follow him that far, and nobody here is asked to. But the part anyone can use is narrower. It's the doubled suffering, the sense that this, unlike everyone else's, shouldn't have happened, that the world has made an exception of you. Often the wise, steady friend who knows exactly what to say about broken cups is already in the room. It's you, talking to someone else. The trick is to turn around and say it to yourself, with the same warmth. It's strangely close to the old rule about loving your neighbor as yourself, only running backward. Treat yourself, for a moment, as you'd treat your neighbor. These things happen. To them. To you.
screen: `LEARN FROM WHERE WE AGREE.` · `ANOTHER'S CUP: THESE THINGS HAPPEN.` · `THE HARDER CASE.` · `SAY IT TO YOURSELF, WARMLY.` · then, large: `THESE THINGS HAPPEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one manageable trouble of your own, a mistake, a breakage, a bad week, and imagine a friend telling you that exact story as if it happened to them. Let your words for them come, kind and steady. Then turn them around and say them to yourself, in the same tone: these things happen.
Cup. When a neighbor's breaks, Epictetus says, we're quick with calm and good advice; turn that same wisdom on your own. Today's word.
Your line: these things happen. The kind friend was in the room all along. Day three hundred fifty-eight, done.
